procedural_history.impugned_order: Order passed by the High Court of Gujarat rejecting the appellant's application for grant of parole under Rule 19 of the Prisons (Bombay Furlough and Parole) Rules, 1959.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court rejected the appellant's application for parole.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, aggrieved by the High Court's order rejecting his parole application, filed an appeal before the Supreme Court. During the appeal, the Supreme Court also took note of the appellant's pending application for remission under Section 432(2) of the CrPC, which was not being considered by the State Government. The Supreme Court issued a notice regarding the remission application and directed its expeditious decision. The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the condition providing for arrest and automatic revocation of remission of sentence if appellant commits any other cognizable offence or inflicts any serious injury to any citizen or property after his release, valid:

facts: The appellant was granted remission of his sentence subject to certain conditions.

One condition (condition no. 2) stated that if the appellant commits any cognizable offense or inflicts serious injury to any person or property after his release, he would be arrested and the remission would be automatically revoked, requiring him to serve the remainder of his sentence.
The appellant challenged this condition, arguing that it was illegal because even a false allegation could lead to the automatic cancellation of his remission.
law: Under Section 432(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), the government has the power to grant remission with or without conditions.
Citing the precedent in *Shaikh Abdul Azees*, the Court affirmed that a breach of a remission condition does not lead to an automatic revival of the sentence.
The government has the discretion to cancel the remission for a breach but is not legally obligated to do so.
Before cancelling a remission, the principles of natural justice must be followed, which include issuing a show-cause notice, providing an opportunity to be heard, and passing a reasoned order.
The decision to cancel remission is subject to judicial review under Article 226 of the Constitution.
application: The Court applied the legal principles to condition no. 2 and determined that it could not be interpreted to mean that every allegation of a breach would automatically lead to the cancellation of remission.
It held that the mere registration of a cognizable offense is not, in itself, a sufficient ground for cancellation. The allegations cannot be taken at face value and must be substantiated.

The Court mandated that the government must consider the nature, seriousness, and gravity of the alleged breach on a case-by-case basis. A minor or trifling breach cannot be a ground for cancellation.
Therefore, the power to revoke remission for a breach of this condition is not absolute or automatic; it must be exercised judiciously and in compliance with natural justice.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the condition was only partly valid. It did not strike down the condition itself but invalidated the provision for 'automatic' revocation. The Court clarified that while the government can impose such a condition, the cancellation of remission is not automatic upon an allegation of a breach. Any action to cancel remission must be based on the seriousness of the breach and must follow the principles of natural justice, including a proper inquiry and a reasoned decision.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the condition providing for arrest and automatic revocation of remission of sentence if appellant commits any other cognizable offence or inflicts any serious injury to any citizen or property after his release, valid:
appellant_arguments: The impugned conditions defeat the very object of the grant of remission.
Putting such a condition confers arbitrary power on the State Government to cancel the remission order.
The condition violates Article 21 of the Constitution of India.
respondent_arguments: Under sub-section (1) of Section 432 of the CrPC, the appropriate Government has the power to remit the whole or any part of the punishment subject to certain conditions.
The provision requires the convict to accept the said conditions, without which he cannot be granted the benefit of remission.
A convict is not entitled to remission of the sentence as a matter of right; the limited right of the convict is only to be considered for remission.
The power to remit sentence is a discretionary power which has to be exercised on public interest considerations.
The appellant has accepted the conditions imposed on him and has furnished surety in terms of the condition.

cases.principle: Conditions imposed must be fair, reasonable and stand the test of scrutiny of Article 14 of the Constitution and cannot be arbitrary as it will violate rights guaranteed under Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The conditions imposed must be fair, reasonable and stand the test of scrutiny of Article 14 of the Constitution – Conditions cannot be arbitrary as it will violate rights guaranteed under Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution.
obiter: Insofar as the exercise of power under sub-section (1) of Section 432 of the CrPC is concerned, the Constitution Bench in the case of V. Sriharan has approved the view taken by this Court in the case of Mohinder Singh v. State of Punjab.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The condition allowing for the revocation of remission if a convict commits another cognizable offense is not automatically invalid, but its enforcement cannot be automatic. The mere registration of a cognizable offense is not a sufficient ground for cancellation. Instead, the principles of natural justice must be read into the process, requiring a show-cause notice, an opportunity to be heard, and a reasoned order from the adjudicating authority. The decision to cancel remission must be made on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the seriousness and gravity of the new offense or breach.
legal_tests_applied: Conditions imposed for remission must be fair, reasonable and stand the test of scrutiny of Article 14 of the Constitution, as arbitrary conditions violate rights guaranteed under Articles 14 and 21.

The principles of natural justice must be read into sub-section (3) of Section 432 of the CrPC, making a show-cause notice, an opportunity to reply and be heard, and a reasoned order essential before the cancellation of remission.
why_appellant_lost: The court did not strike down the condition in its entirety, upholding the State's power to cancel remission if a convict commits a new offense. The power to grant remission is discretionary and can be conditioned on future good behavior, which includes not committing serious crimes.
why_respondent_won: The court affirmed the State's fundamental power to cancel a granted remission if the convict breaches the conditions by committing another cognizable offense or inflicting serious injury, thereby upholding the substance of the condition.
policy_considerations: The decision to grant remission has to be well-informed, reasonable and fair to all concerned, and cannot be sought by a convict as a matter of right.
Factors including public interest, the gravity and nature of the offenses, and the antecedents of the convict are relevant considerations for the discretionary power to grant remission.
To prevent the arbitrary exercise of power, the existence of a rational policy for granting remission is necessary.
A convict whose remission has been cancelled can always adopt a remedy under Article 226 of the Constitution of India to challenge the cancellation order.
